motion: Is the Canaanite conquest morally defensible as an act commanded by a loving God?

bridges.description: Connect conquest judgment to the loving yet judging God revealed across both Testaments.
Use ancient war rhetoric to limit literal total-destruction readings.
Identify military centers and corrupting institutions rather than ethnicity as the target.
Defend a unique contextual judgment without making it repeatable.
Argue that residual civilian killing or forced group removal remains morally indefensible.
Concede exaggeration while denying that it removes the moral residue.
Use Jesus and moral intuition as controls on conquest readings.
Offer historically cautious, spiritualized, and moral-error alternatives.

sections.title: Scripture and interpretive method
sections.rationale: The rival Christian hermeneutics determine how conquest commands bear on divine love.

sections.title: Historicity and war rhetoric
sections.rationale: Historical caution and exaggerated war language determine the literal scope.

sections.title: Civilian harm and moral responsibility
sections.rationale: Noncombatant targeting is the central moral dispute.

sections.title: Identity removal, herem, and genocide
sections.rationale: The parties dispute the object and moral classification of the campaign.

sections.title: Christological alternatives and exceptional judgment
sections.rationale: The final statements directly test divine love, alternative readings, and contextual exception.
